person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Consistent with our expectation (H,), when whites are asked about locking up violent inner-city criminals, their policy preferences are based much more strongly on their racial attitudes.

span.label: racial code-word framing of crime policy opinion
span.quote: What follows is a systematic analysis of the impact of a phrase believed by many to carry strong racial connotations: "inner city."

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: We do so by embedding an experiment in a national survey of whites, where a random half of respondents was asked whether they support spending money for prisons (versus antipoverty programs) to lock up "violent criminals," while the other half was asked about "violent inner city criminals."

span.label: The authors do not claim their frame is the subtlest possible racial cue; many respondents openly equate the inner city with black Americans.
span.quote: We cannot, of course, claim that the inner-city frame is the most subtle of all possible racial frames, as evidenced by our finding (see footnote 4) that many clearly equate the inner city with blacks.

span.label: The design tests policy preferences only; extension to candidate preferences is asserted but untested.
span.quote: While our research has focused on policy preferences, we see no reason why we would not obtain the same results if we focused on candidate preferences-a topic for future analysis.

span.label: The analysis is restricted to white respondents; the African-American subsample was dropped for lack of variance on the outcome.
span.quote: The study also included a sample (N = 579) of African-American respondents who were not used in this analysis, in part because there was virtually no variation in responses to the dependent measure among African-Americans, who overwhelmingly rejected the prison option regardless of experimental condition.

span.label: THE EFFECT IS NOT A SHIFT IN THE ANSWER - IT IS A CHANGE IN WHAT PREDICTS IT. `Whites' racial attitudes (for example, racial stereotypes) were MUCH MORE IMPORTANT IN SHAPING PREFERENCES for punitive policies when they receive the racially coded, `inner city` question.` The outcome here is a REGRESSION COEFFICIENT, not a mean or a latency: the same people, the same policy question, and a different thing driving their answer depending on two words. **A corpus that stores `prime -> outcome, direction: increases` cannot express this at all** - the direction is not up or down, it is `your prior attitudes now matter more to what you say`
span.quote: Consistent with the literature on issue framing, we find that whites' racial attitudes (for example, racial stereotypes) were much more important in shaping preferences for punitive policies when they receive the racially coded

span.label: THE SMALLEST PRIME IN THIS CORPUS, AND THE AUTHORS SAY SO DELIBERATELY: `We have carried IMPLICITNESS TO ITS EXTREME: we have used NO VISUALS, NO MENTION OF RACE, and NO MENTION OF CHARACTERISTICS often associated with race (like `welfare queens`).` Two words inserted into one survey item. Every other prime in this corpus is a word list, an image, a scent, a room, a sentence structure or a period of noise; this is a modifier. **And the minimalism is the argument** - the paper's point is that after the Willie Horton ad made blatant appeals costly, what remains available is this small
span.quote: We have carried implicitness to its extreme: we have used no visuals, no mention of race, and no mention of characteristics often associated with race

span.label: THE CAUSAL CLAIM IS EXACT BECAUSE THE DESIGN IS THAT SIMPLE: `Because of the very simple experimental design employed, in which differences between the inner-city and the baseline group CAN ONLY BE ATTRIBUTED TO THE INTRODUCTION OF THE CODE WORD, it seems clear that respondents who think about criminals from the inner city have been encouraged to evaluate anticrime policies on the basis of the group that they associate with inner cities.` **The inference chain is stated in full and each link is separable** - the two words differ, therefore the difference is theirs, therefore the group was brought to mind, therefore the policy was judged by the group. `It seems clear` marks where the demonstration ends and the interpretation begins
span.quote: Because of the very simple experimental design employed, in which differences between the inner-city and the baseline group can only be attributed to the introduction of the code word, it seems clear that respondents who think about criminals from the inner city have been encouraged to evaluate anticrime policies on the basis of the group that they associate with inner cities

span.label: IMPLICIT BEATS EXPLICIT, AND THAT IS AN EMPIRICAL CLAIM ABOUT PERSUASION RATHER THAN ABOUT COGNITION: a blatant message `would, today, be either UNPRODUCTIVE OR COUNTERPRODUCTIVE because, as a number of studies suggest, IMPLICIT APPEALS ARE MUCH MORE EFFECTIVE.` Most of this corpus treats implicitness as a methodological device for isolating automatic processing. Here it is a STRATEGIC property with a history: the Willie Horton ad made the explicit version expensive, so the implicit one is what survives
span.quote: Most likely, such a message would, today, be either unproductive or counterproductive because, as a number of studies suggest, implicit appeals are much more effective

span.label: builds-on → Nelson and Kinder (1996), group-centric issue framing
span.quote: Most generally, they are fully consistent with, and add to, the literature on issue framing-particularly the literature focusing on the group-centric nature of a frame (Nelson and Kinder 1996).

span.label: extends → Mendelberg (2001), implicit/explicit racial appeals and the Willie Horton ad
span.quote: Put differently, it may have helped transform what Mendelberg terms an "implicit" appeal into a more explicit appeal that would, doubtless, be recognized for its blatant racial component today.

span.label: builds-on → Druckman (2001), limits of elite framing
span.quote: Thus, while our findings provide ample evidence of the power of racial coding to affect citizens' judgments, they are also consistent with recent studies that demonstrate that there are limits to the ability of elites to use frames to manipulate mass opinion (Druckman 2001).

span.label: issue framing —causes→ racial attitudes
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — **NO `effect_direction`, AND THIS IS THE CLEAREST CASE YET FOR WHY THAT AXIS DOES NOT FIT EVERY EDGE.** The code word does not increase or reduce racial attitudes - it increases how much they PREDICT the policy answer. The vocabulary has no term for `raises the weight of`, and `increases` would be read as `makes people more prejudiced`, which is not what was measured and would be a serious misreading of a paper about race. Weight 0.9: the design supports the causal claim, and the quantity it acts on needs the note.

span.label: issue framing —part-of→ code words
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — The paper places its own result inside the group-centric framing literature rather than claiming a new mechanism - `fully consistent with, and add to, the literature on issue framing`. `part-of` reads the code word as the smallest instance of a frame. Weight 0.85: this span is the paper's placement of itself, which is a claim about a literature and not a result. Note the OCR `modem` for `modern` - the paper's own scan, left as it stands.
span.quote: This analysis has been designed to address, in the most specific fashion possible, racialized code words in modem political discourse. The findings, we believe, are highly informative in a number of different ways. Most generally, they are fully consistent with, and add to, the literature on issue framing-particularly the literature focusing on the group-centric nature of a frame (Nelson and Kinder 1996). When messages are framed in such a way to reinforce the relationship between a particular policy and a particular group, it becomes far more likely that individuals will evaluate the policy on the basis of their evaluations of the group
